book: 095 - Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor
essays: 1. Finding the Meaning of Life in Downton Abbey
2. I May Be a Socialist, But I’m Not a Lunatic
4. Finding One’s Place and Being Useful
8. Lie Is So Unmusical a Word
10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna
12. Should We Really Care about the Crawleys
13. Topophilia; or, How We Got Hooked on Downton
14. Things Can Happen that Nobody Could Imagine Only a Few Years Ago
15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is
16. Female Integrity in Times of Change
samples: The book's introduction argues that Downton Abbey's genius is letting universal moral and social realities burst forth in particular incidents: the snuffbox affair makes Thomas a classic villain (stealing, defaming Bates) and Bates a Christ-, Socrates-, or Confucius-type innocent, showing that moral clarity is beautiful rather than superficial. It reads the Thomas-Bates-Grantham hierarchy as an invitation to think about 'greater and lesser,' tying propriety (Confucius), dharma, and justice (Aristotle) to paying attention to social difference, which Western viewers raised on equality find foreign yet intriguing. It closes by insisting the characters are more complex than their types - Thomas takes a beating to spare Jimmy, Bates may have killed outside the law - and previews the volume's themes of Humean 'small morals' (etiquette), women's rights, work, place, and war.

Blessing tests the Steve Jobs/Oprah 'do what you love' creed against Downton, where rigid class structure assigns nearly everyone a role they did not choose. She distinguishes happiness from meaningfulness (Matthew's war wounds, Mary's grief after his death) and purposefulness (Grantham's custodian speech), then weighs subjectivist theories of meaning, including Nietzsche's idea that meaning arises from the passionate process itself, against Nozick's permanence view and Susan Wolf's hybrid 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness,' adding Kant's duty to develop one's talents against a world of idle pleasure. She concludes that the Abbey's ethos - Grantham as custodian not owner, Carson's pride in service, Patmore's kitchen, 'I have no right to be unhappy' - shows that socially necessary work one does not love can still make a meaningful life, while DWYL is elitist and narcissistic.

Walderczak stages the Branson-Robert-Matthew triangle as socialism, aristocratic conservatism, and capitalism colliding over the estate's duty to its people. He tracks how Tom's Marx-flavored socialism - really closer to Owen's and Fourier's utopian cooperatism - evaporates once he marries Sybil and co-manages the land, the chauffeur 'Branson' becoming family-member 'Tom,' a case of David Harvey's capitalist pacification. Meanwhile Robert's noblesse oblige - secretly paying a tenant's overdue rent from private funds, ranting 'profits, profits, profits,' treating ownership as custodianship of the tenants - leaves the author asking who the real socialist is, and answering that Robert's conservatism has far more in common with socialist ideals than Tom's self-confessed politics ever did.

Wills uses Georg Simmel's The Philosophy of Money to argue Matthew's two-season arc is a corruption story rather than a romance: the principled middle-class lawyer who vows Downton will not change him, calls valeting 'a very silly occupation,' and wants to dress himself gradually lets wealth enchant him, dodges reviewing the entail, and returns for Mary. He reads the Mary-Matthew match as an economic transaction that neatly solves the succession problem - money as the aristocracy's toy, Mary becoming part of the deal - against Anna and Bates's money-free courtship as the show's only genuinely loving relationship. The chapter ends by turning Simmel's warning on the audience: we root for the couple because we are as powerless before wealth's charm, and as greedy for it, as Matthew is.

Karavitis argues that work, not social class, is Downton's real theme, sorting characters in a two-by-two matrix of class membership against acceptance or rejection of the existing social order. Those who accept their place stagnate - Violet ('We don't work,' 'What is a weekend?'), Robert the mismanaging custodian, the perpetually jobless Molesley - while those who reject it flourish: Isobel's drive to be 'useful,' Sybil's nursing ('I feel useful for the first time in my life'), Gwen's hidden typewriter, Alfred's Ritz training. He surveys Rousseau on work's role in inequality, Smith on the division of labor, and Marx on labor and ideology on the negative side, and Aristotle, Russell's 'In Praise of Idleness,' and Pieper on leisure and personal projects on the positive side, ending with the prediction that automation will soon give everyone the Crawley daughters' problem of what to do with a life without work.

Dougherty argues that at Downton manners are not incidental etiquette but a central means of demonstrating moral character and respect. Matthew's shift from calling valeting 'a very silly occupation for a grown man' to valuing Molesley's role shows decorum tracking his growing respect; Branson's tweed suit at white-tie dinners and 'uniforms of oppression' display disrespect even where his politics are sound; Sir Richard's parting boorishness betrays a lack of moral character; and the Dowager Countess's polished barbs prove manners can serve as a mask for self-interest rather than virtue. The framework combines Nancy Sherman's 'aesthetic of character,' Aristotle's person of extraordinary virtue whose goodness must appear in particular ways, and Sarah Buss's idea that good manners constantly remind us that others are worthy of respect.

book: 096 - Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter
essays: 3. What’s So Bad about Eating People
9. Not Knowing Serial Killers with Hannibal Lecktor
12. A Little Empathy for Hannibal Is a Dangerous Thing
14. A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Dinner Party
17. The Beguiling Horror of Hannibal Lecter
samples: This opening page is the book's front matter of advance-praise blurbs (Mikita Brottman, Sara Waller, Cynthia Freeland, Harold Schechter and others), not an essay. The blurbs preview the volume's themes - the morality of eating people, Lecter's psychiatry and empathy, aesthetics and haute cuisine, friendship, evil, and why we are drawn to a cultured cannibal across Harris's novels, the five films, and the television series - while dropping the names of Plato, Augustine, Nietzsche, and Foucault without developing any of them. No philosophical argument is made here, so no slugs apply.

Le Menu is the book's own table of contents, styled as a multi-course dinner menu running from Apéritif (Westfall's 'Hello, Dr. Lecter') through Café ('Doctor, Heal Thyself'), with the six parts titled by Lecter quotations such as 'Having an Old Friend for Dinner' and 'I Gave You a Rare Gift, but You Didn't Want It'. It lists the eighteen essays and their authors plus the back-matter resources and index, and argues nothing itself.

Westfall's introduction sorts Lecter's incarnations into four presentations: the psychopath (Brian Cox's 'Lecktor' in Manhunter, modeled on Harris's real-life Mexican prison doctor 'Dr. Salazar'), the anti-hero avenging Mischa in Hannibal Rising, the vampire (Hopkins's Silence of the Lambs Lecter as a Dracula figure who feeds from a sense of innate superiority), and the devil (Mikkelsen's fallen angel, Romula's 'Shaitan', wielder of the church-collapse argument that God enjoys killing). What unites them is a Nietzschean self-conception - Lecter as an Übermensch to whom ordinary law and morality do not apply - and a Socratic function: like Socrates in the Phaedrus, he goads Will, Clarice, and the audience into examining what we already are, posing questions he never resolves because each of us must take the 'rare gift' for ourselves.

Staged as a fictional interview over herring and aquavit in Copenhagen, Wong lets Lecter wield philosophical critique like an 'autopsy saw' - he invokes Schopenhauer's condemnation of anthropophagy and Montaigne's noble-savage view only to have the interviewer refuse both, and 'creams Aristotle' in a debate about categories - before she adopts Agamben's distinction between sovereigns and bare life. Lecter's 'we are elaborations of carbon' de-anthropocentrism, his killing of the rude, and the parallel cases of shipwrecked sailors who ate shipmates, Guantánamo detainees, and drone casualties all serve her argument that every political order rests on someone arbitrarily deciding which lives are mere killable matter, and that Lecter horrifies because he shows every human is also nonhuman - Us and Them at once.

Westfall sorts cannibalism into starvation types (the Donner Party, the Andes rugby team, Alferd Packer, and Grutas's crew killing Mischa - 'We have to eat or die'), cultural types (Aztec ritual eating, the prisoner-eating tribes of Montaigne's essay, whom Montaigne judged no worse than the French torturing their prisoners alive, and Neanderthal nutritional eating), and hedonistic types (paraphilic, sadistic, and recreational). Using Irvine's active/passive distinction he argues that it is the killing, not the eating, that makes cannibalism wrong - passive consumption of corpses is at worst distasteful - while Lecter emerges as a purely recreational cannibal who eats 'because he likes it', and the TV series' dinner parties turn Jack and Will from unwitting 'benign cannibals' into morally responsible passive ones.

McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.

book: 097 - The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More
essays: Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right
Walker Bite. If I Don’t Save the World, I Have No Value
10. We’re Not Free to Save Lee
12. They Just Want Me to Be Like Them
samples: Wayne Yuen's introduction argues that philosophy needs extreme scenarios to stress-test moral, political, and religious theories, and that The Walking Dead supplies two: the reanimation of the dead and the collapse of social, political, and economic order. He frames the book around the show's most overt question - why be moral at all when survival pushes against it, as with Rick's compromises and the choice between searching for a missing girl or writing her off as having 'looked at the flowers' - plus how religion fares when the dead rise, and the string of attempted societies (the Prison, Woodbury, Terminus, Grady Memorial, Alexandria) that mirror our own world of failing nations and unjust rule. The essays, he says, hold a mirror to our values: we can become the walking dead without any zombies.

Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'

Cowan uses Jenner's suicide in the exploding CDC (1.6 'TS-19') to pose Camus's question 'Why should I not commit suicide?', and rejects Jenner's despair the Camusian way: Michonne in 4.9 'After' - slaying her own walker look-alike and then her two pet walkers - is his Sisyphus in revolt, unlike Gareth, whose revolt lacks the respect for human dignity that makes Sisyphus happy. He then objects that Camus never explains why human life has intrinsic dignity in a godless universe, noting that Sartrean authenticity could equally license the Governor's Woodbury experiments or Gareth's cannibalism, and turns to Hershel's providential hope as the religious alternative. Following Plantinga, he argues belief in God can be properly basic through a sensus divinitatis - Hershel seeing God's hand in 2.4 'Cherokee Rose' and the tornado-spared barn of 5.10 'Them' - so if God exists, Jenner was not right.

Seth Walker asks what makes a life worth saving, testing the show's survival choices against instrumental value (usefulness to the group) and Tom Regan's subject-of-a-life criterion of inherent value. Shane's sacrifice of Otis for Carl, Lori's fatal pregnancy and Judith's birth, the Governor's obsession with Meghan, and the hunts for Sophia all show that neither usefulness nor Regan's equal, non gradated inherent value explains why children are selectively elevated - and perceived 'innocence' fails with the colder Carl and with Lizzie. He concludes with Bob Stookey's line in 4.10 'Inmates' ('Not everything has to mean something... but it can'): following Sartre's claim that man is nothing but what he makes of himself, the survivors are condemned to be free and must make their survival mean something, as Daryl and Carol's search for Sophia did.

Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.

Hawkes uses Rick's bar confrontation with Dave and Tony in 2.8 'Nebraska' to ask when lying is right, after defining lying through the Governor's white flag at the National Guard camp and Eugene's false cure claim. He rejects moral relativism - the Claimers' rules, Terminus's 'butcher or cattle', the Governor's 'we will do the only thing' - because it forbids criticizing rapists and cannibals and erases moral progress, then finds utilitarianism shaky given Eugene's unforeseen deadly consequences and Rick's refusal to hand Michonne to the Governor at 'Arrow on the Doorpost.' He defends a duty-based deontology in which the duty to protect the farm overrides the duty not to lie, and closes with Robert Kirkman's own lie about an alien invasion that got The Walking Dead published.

book: 098 - The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!
essays: Hello, My Name is Inigo Montoya. You Bought This Book. Prepare to Enjoy!
2. Why Men of Action Don’t Lie
4. That Moron Aristotle on the Means of Persuasion
5. Does It Mean What Vizzini Thinks It Means
7. Who Should Have Won the Battle of Wits
10. Making the Punishment Fit the Crime
11. Have Fun Overthrowing This Evil Government!
12. Should I Really Stop That Rhyming
16. My Name Is—Hang on, What Was It Meant to Be Again Are You Sure Well, Okay Then . .
18. I Know Something You Don’t Know
19. The Medical Ethics of Miracle Max
samples: The collection's introduction, written as a parody of the movie's bedtime-story frame: a man claiming to be both the sixteenth Dread Pirate Roberts and a descendant of S. Morgenstern tells the editors how the adventures of the Man in Black, Inigo, Fezzik, Buttercup, Prince Humperdinck, and Miracle Max teach lessons in logic, metaphysics, ethics, philosophy of language, and political philosophy. It repeats Vizzini's boast that Plato, Aristotle, and Socrates were morons (whom the philosophers 'weren't buying') and jokes that everything is 'inconceivable!' - 'I do not think it means what he thinks it means' - before closing with 'As you wish!'

Fallis argues the movie is really about lying and duplicity, not true love: Humperdinck frames Guilder for Buttercup's abduction, the Dread Pirate Roberts is a serial persona, and even the heroes bluff their way into the castle. He treats this as 'adversarial epistemology,' showing that Descartes's malicious demon and Kant's argument that universalized lying is impossible only rule out extreme scenarios and cannot unmask mundane deceivers like Vizzini and Humperdinck (a point he sharpens with Parfit's objection that liars sometimes profitably tell the truth). What does real work are Hume's tools for evaluating testimony: Valerie catches Miracle Max lying about 'to blave' by asking what he has to gain, and Buttercup catches Humperdinck when his claim that every ship in the armada will accompany the honeymoon contradicts his promise of the four fastest ships.

Mahon maps the film's non-romantic relationships onto Aristotle's philia: the loyal friendship of Inigo and Fezzik under Vizzini's abuse, expanded into a four-person 'family' once Westley, who defeated and spared them with respect, joins them to storm the castle. He argues deception in the film tracks the absence of philia - bad men incapable of friendship (Vizzini, Humperdinck, Rugen) lie to anyone, while friends never lie to each other and the early duels are sportsmanlike. Westley's line 'We are men of action. Lies do not become us' encodes an honor code that real men do not lie to real men even when enemies (hence Westley cheats Vizzini in the Battle of Wits with both goblets poisoned, and the chapter analyzes the resulting triple- and quadruple-bluff regress), while the one exception - Westley letting Buttercup stay deceived about Humperdinck - exposes the code's chauvinism, matching Aristotle's view that philia in its purest form exists only between male equals.

Alloy reads the whole story as being about promises - Westley's 'I will always come for you,' Humperdinck's insincerely made and casually broken vows to Buttercup, and Inigo's vow of vengeance to his murdered father. He tests conventionalism, using Rawls's idea that breaking a promise cheats on a fair rule-bound practice (illustrated by Inigo's rule-governed duel and the Battle of Wits where both parties cheat), against expectationalism, on which obligation comes from the trust and expectations created, as when Humperdinck manipulates Buttercup through her trust. Both theories struggle with Inigo's promise to a dead man, so Alloy argues with Searle that it is responsibility for intent that makes a promise, and defends his own view - against the Hobbesian consensus - that every promise is also a self-promise whose binding force is the promisor's self-respect: promises 'make us people.'

Wolfe applies Aristotle's definition of rhetoric - seeing the available means of persuasion, where success depends on the speaker's character, the audience's emotional state, and the argument's content - to show that Westley is the story's master rhetorician while Humperdinck is a poor one. Humperdinck fails by coasting on his title ('I am your Prince and you will marry me'), whereas Westley plays on Inigo's mind during the cliff climb, demoralizes him with the left-handed switch, neutralizes Fezzik's strength with a chokehold, exploits Vizzini's overconfidence in the Battle of Wits, and reverses the 'to the pain' situation by targeting Humperdinck's cowardice and vanity. The chapter also sets Aristotle's neutral view of rhetoric against Socrates's suspicion of it as sophistry (relented from in the Phaedrus).

Fetterman takes Inigo's 'I do not think it means what you think it means' seriously and defends Vizzini: the line may merely record that two speakers define 'inconceivable' differently, or react to it differently. Using Wittgenstein, he argues communication requires agreement in judgments, so Vizzini and Inigo may simply be playing different language games, like users of two different dictionaries. He then runs Wittgenstein's private language argument against the possibility that Vizzini's usage is correct by his own idiosyncratic rules - a purely private definition could never be confirmed or be wrong, since only Vizzini checks it - and touches on the philosophical sense of 'conceivable' as logically possible (the square circle) and the group language game that lets everyone accept Miracle Max's 'to blave.'

book: 099 - Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored
essays: The “Other Shit” that Louis C.K. Wanted to Talk About
3. When to Hate and When to Be Irate
4. On Being a Dead Person Who Hasn’t Died Yet
8. Should Jane Get to Be Bored
9. What Fuckin’ Chance Does a Kid Have
19. The Playful Thought Experiments of Louis C.K
samples: Editor Mark Ralkowski's introduction argues that Louis C.K. moved from absurdist joke-writing to 'personal revelation comedy,' the 'other shit' about love, death, boredom, sex, and parenting that he now builds his specials and Louie around. Framed by Trevor Griffiths's play Comedians, it stages the choice between comedy as entertainment ('coloured sweeties') and comedy as medicine that dares to see the truths audiences fear, and claims Louis chose the latter - developing each hour by the samurai-sword process of constant folding and reworking, opening with his strongest bit, and trading money to FX for total creative control. The chapter maps no individual philosophers; it sets up the book's thesis that Louis's bits are worth philosophical reading.

Max Elder reads Louis through Nietzsche's Gay Science claim that all philosophy is unconscious memoir, arguing Louis's confession-like comedy reveals dark truths we would rather flee - the Conan 'everything's amazing and nobody's happy' bit, the 'I know the darkness' exchange with the Christian woman, and the Subway/Pamela scene where a homeless man bathes behind a subway violinist. Using Nietzsche's line that man alone laughs because he suffers so deeply, and The Birth of Tragedy's comic as the artistic discharge of the nausea of absurdity, the chapter argues Louis's laughter performs a gestalt switch that ties the ugly to the beautiful and so redeems it. It reads the religions-supply-meaning argument - God's mockery-laughter versus Nietzsche's holy laughter - as the reason redemption now happens in comedy clubs rather than churches, and closes with Louie's 'Country Drive' scolding of Jane ('you don't get to be bored') as Nietzschean embrace of the amazing fact of being alive.

John Heaney pairs Louis with Schopenhauer: both see human existence as error-shaped misery, but more importantly both treat sex as the will-to-live tricking the intellect into serving the species while we mistake the species' good for our own. He reads the 'Come on, God' stand-up (every beautiful thought about a woman followed by a disgusting one) and Louie's 'So Old/Playdate' speech that 'sex is really trying to have a family' as comedic versions of Schopenhauer's metaphysics of love, with episodes like 'Bummer/Blueberries' (a decapitation killing Louie's lust mid-non-date), 'Elevator Part 4' (the civil divorce flashback ending in a possible pregnancy), and 'Eddie' (a man losing the will-to-live along with the will-to-love) enacting the oscillation between sexual arousal and suicidal despair. Even Louis's devotion to his daughters fits Schopenhauer's claim that the sexual delusion transfers to offspring, which is why 'Eddie' ends with Louie refusing to name his reasons to live - he has to pick up his kids in the morning.

Daniel Alloy opens with Aristotle's demand that one be angry 'as and when and for as long as one ought' and builds a theory distinguishing anger (a response to a specific offense, seeking proportional payback) from hatred (a response to a thing's very existence, seeking its destruction). He tests the theory on Louis's bits - hating deer as a class and fantasizing about giving them AIDS, the six-year-old 'Jizzanthapuss,' the Pig Newtons fight with a three-year-old, the Cinnabon clerk, the 'Awesome Possum' hipster, and the justified driver who yells 'suck a sack of dicks.' He argues justified hatred is impossible, since it would require a pure-malevolence being that could not be an autonomous person, so hatred is always wrong while properly proportioned anger remains a necessary part of the moral life. Kant supplies the self-respect dimension ('one who makes himself a worm cannot complain if people step on him'): failing to get angry at real wrongs done to you or your children signals a character deficiency, not virtue.

Mark Ralkowski argues that Louis's 'dead people who haven't died yet' bit sounds like Marcus Aurelius, and that Dr. Bigelow's Season Four advice about back pain, the three-legged dog, and heartbreak works as the Stoic spiritual exercises Pierre Hadot described - above all the 'view from above' that re-describes things to strip them to their true value. Epictetus's dichotomy of control explains Bigelow's core advice: pain is not 'up to us' but our judgments about it are, so Louie should adjust his expectations to nature ('every second without back pain is a lucky second') instead of demanding a pain-free life. The apparently un-Stoic counsel to savor heartbreak ('misery is wasted on the miserable') is defended as genuinely Stoic: viewing his lost love from the perspective of a dead-person-who-hasn't-died-yet, Louie can accept sadness as precious and impermanent rather than being crushed by it. The chapter concedes Louis is no philosopher, but suggests his bits - contrasted with Seinfeld's 'polished' version on Talking Funny - can be read as newly discovered Meditations for comedy audiences.

Bekka Williams argues that Louis's 'just want a shitty body' bit restates Epictetus's central Stoic teaching - want events to happen as they do happen, because only judgments, efforts, and desires are 'up to us' while bodies, reputations, and outcomes are not. She reads the Late Show arc (Tardigan's non-offer of the job, then Louie's triumphant 'Hey Letterman, I did it!' when Letterman stays) as Epictetus's cardplayer ideal: total effort on what is controllable, calm acceptance of what is not, alongside the bits about disgusting bodies, 'do the shit out of your job,' Jane and the mango pop, and Louis's self-trained habit of intercepting impulsive desires like the motorcycle urge. Like Epictetus, Louis is presented as a truth-teller who corrects mistaken impressions even when it is unpleasant, and the chapter uses him to rebut the charge that Stoicism means not caring.

book: 100 - Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_
essays: 1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone
samples: The editor's introduction reframes the Batman-versus-Superman brawl: what fans are really arguing about is not strength but who is the better hero and "who should we try to be like." Michaud recalls learning sacrifice and persistence from Burton's Batman and total self-giving from the Death of Superman, and frames the book's choice as hope in humanity versus cynical vigilance about what people could become. He promises that the assembled philosophers flatly disagree and leaves the verdict of the fight to the reader.

Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.

Malloy asks whether the two law-breaking vigilantes are criminals and whether any duty to obey the law survives scrutiny. He runs consent theory through Superman surrendering in handcuffs in Man of Steel and the Red Son Superman's residence in the USSR, uses Darkseid's Apokolips as Hobbes's security sovereign against Locke's natural-rights limits, deploys Hume against tacit consent (Batman would never leave Gotham even in No Man's Land), and dismantles gratitude theory (the Kents' adoption involved a sacrificial choice the law cannot make) and fair play (Nozick's Batman-lottery undercuts "I'm not wearing hockey pads"). He lands near Wolff-style philosophical anarchism: Superman's constrained lawbreaking endorses the law's legitimacy while Batman treats law as one more tool in his war, making him a force of chaos.

Springett applies evolutionary biology to the matchup: comparing fitness, adaptations, and arms races (Batman's escalating gadget war with his rogues versus Superman facing no competition at all), he concludes Superman is objectively fitter, while on the technical definition of altruism Batman is more altruistic than the invulnerable Superman, who cannot lower his own fitness. Redefining a "Superhero" as an individual who effectively raises the fitness of many others, and adding Gould's catastrophist view that species extinction is the norm, he argues a planet with Superman keeps the whole species alive through catastrophes Batman could never avert. He explicitly rejects Social Darwinism - Superman is its counterexample because he saves the less fit - and, with Dawkins, credits conscious awareness with letting us choose our own goals, crowning Superman the superior Superhero.

Farrell traces the heroes' knightly nicknames (Dark Knight, Caped Crusader, Man of Steel) to medieval chivalry as C.S. Lewis defines it in "The Necessity of Chivalry": the knight's double demand to be both stern and meek, each "to the nth degree," with knightly character a work of art achieved rather than a gift of nature. Both heroes show the split (playboy Bruce versus Spartan Batman in Batman Begins, meek Clark versus bold Superman), and both go to extremes - Batman's interrogation-room brutality in The Dark Knight, Superman turning back time for Lois in Superman: The Movie - but Lewis's hardest test is the mighty man who restrains himself. Superman's lifelong self-restraint, contrasted with uninhibited red-kryptonite Clark in Smallville's "Red," makes him the truer modern knight.

LaBauve opens with a staged Justice League debate over rescuing the Joker's hostages, where Batman's emotional, vengeance-tinged appeal loses to Superman's trust-based plea, and reads it through Aristotle's On Rhetoric: Batman persuades almost entirely by pathos (the relatable brokenness of Nolan's trilogy) with detective's logos, while Superman balances pathos, logos, and above all ethos, since Aristotle calls the speaker's character the strongest appeal. Against Max Landis's claim that Superman is irrelevant, he pairs the Death of Superman with Nietzsche's "God is dead" parable and the Kill Bill monologue to argue that Superman is a mythology of virtue - alongside real moral heroes like Gandhi, King, and Jesus - showing humans the ideal they ought to become, so Superman not only wins but must win.

book: 101 - Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems
essays: 1. More Golems around Than You Might Think
2. Golem Morality in the Modern World
3. We Willna Be Fooled Again! Wee Free Anarchists!
4. The Liberating Power of Nanny Ogg’s Bouncing Bosom
5. The Truth Shall Make Ye Fret
8. Honesty Trumps Cleverness Sam Vimes and Commonsense Philosophy
9. Why Would You Put a Con Artist in Charge of the Money
10. Lord Vetinari’s Friendly Guide to Tyranny
11. Can a Leopard Change Its Shorts
12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld
14. Being One’s Me (Witchy) Personal Identity on the Discworld
15. The Serious Monk’s Guide to Re-writing History
17. Sin, My Young Man, Is When You Treat People as Things
18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld
20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork
samples: Using Feet of Clay and Witches Abroad, Froehlich argues we are all like golems: our behavior is driven by the 'words in our heads,' the texts that society and the powerful put there. Lyotard's metanarratives explain how Lily Weatherwax forces Genua to live out fairy-tale plots and how Dragon King of Arms rewrites Nobby's family tree to manufacture a king, while dwarfish gender norms keep Cheery Littlebottom trapped in a culturally imposed text. Freedom comes only when, like Dorfl after Carrot buys him his own receipt, a person rejects the imposed words and chooses words of the heart - 'words in the heart cannot be taken.'

Skene weighs Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' - opened with a River Ankh drowning-child variant - against the golem morality of Going Postal and Feet of Clay. Mr. Pump's charge that Moist von Lipwig's frauds 'hastened the deaths' of 2.338 people grounds a golem standard of actuarial murder that Skene applies to the 2008 banking crisis and Mao's Great Leap Forward. With Kant, the chapter holds that free choice is the foundation of moral responsibility and respect for others' wills, but unlike Singer's unlimited demands, golem morality asks us to own the foreseeable consequences of our choices without sacrificing everything.

Reading The Wee Free Men, Kugler treats the Nac Mac Feegle, Granny Aching, and Tiffany as embodiments of the anarchist suspicion of political authority, staging Nozick's minimal state and spontaneous protective associations against Huemer's philosophical anarchism from The Problem of Political Authority. The Feegles' creed 'Nae quin! Nae king!', their flight from the exploitative Fairy Queen, the Baron's sheep-killing dog compromise, and the mercy shown the lonely kidnapper Miss Robinson all show law treated as a flexible guideline that must yield to love, community, and care for the weak. Kugler concludes that Pratchett romanticizes anarchism: his anarchists win hearts, watching authority from within the system rather than overthrowing it.

Froehlich reads Witches Abroad through Mikhail Bakhtin's theory of carnival and the grotesque from Rabelais and His World: Lily Weatherwax's palace ball is 'high culture' as tyrannical hierarchy, while the Genua street carnival, Nanny Ogg's bouncing bosom, and Baron Saturday's untamable swamp bring grotesque low-culture energy that crashes the ball and shatters Lily's frozen fairy-tale order. Against Bakhtin's pessimism that carnival merely lets the oppressed blow off steam, the chapter argues that Granny Weatherwax and Nanny break the cycle, giving Genua a real chance at self-determined, more fun lives.

Watson uses The Truth - William de Worde's accidental invention of Ankh-Morpork's first newspaper and the plot to frame Lord Vetinari - to stage the three classic arguments for censorship: direct harm (character assassination 'works every day'), indirect harm (with MacKinnon's point that the speech of the dominant drowns out the subordinated, applied to speciesist insults at Koom Valley), and the false-beliefs argument. Against them stand the knowledge problem and the equality assumption: Mrs. Arcanum's deference to print, Vetinari's turtle-shaped-world joke, and the Montessori-Broca dispute show we never know in advance which beliefs are false, and any censor like Lord de Worde has his own agenda. Vetinari's verdict that 'free men pull in all kinds of directions' because 'pulling together is the aim of despotism' carries the chapter's Millian case that free speech is a horrible necessity.

Kempner reads the Luggage - the sapient, homicidal pearwood chest that pursues Rincewind from The Color of Magic through The Light Fantastic and Interesting Times - as the embodiment of Camus's absurd: the 'divorce' between our demand that the world make sense and a world that does not care. Rincewind, who dreams of a rational, scientifically ordered universe while the Disc sails on a turtle and the gods smash atheists' windows, is cast as Sisyphus, and the trolls who 'suffer from philosophy' and freeze solid show where the futile quest for order ends. When Rincewind finally says 'Come on' to the huddled Luggage and readers come to love what once terrified them, the chapter performs Camus's acceptance of the absurd as freedom.

book: 102 - Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA
essays: 3. When Clone Club Looks for Answers
5. The Human Being in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction
7. I Am and Am Not You
8. Laughing in the Face of the Absurd
16. Is Sarah Manning Responsible for What She Does
samples: The editors' introduction retells Sarah Manning's situation: a broke grifter on the run from her drug-dealing ex, she watches her double Beth kill herself on the train platform and steals her identity, which earns her shootings, kidnapping, torture, and the loss of her daughter. It jokes that Sarah's real mistake was not reading this book first, listing its topics — the metaphysics of cloning, personal identity, sisterhood, family, the absurd, Buddhism, feminism, epistemology — as the Mill-style "higher pleasures" that would have prepared her, and ushers the reader on to Chapter 1.

Argues that Project Leda and Castor are a textbook case of Parfit's non-identity problem and its "Implausible Conclusion": Neolution knowingly built the clones barren by design and doomed to fatal illness, yet since none of them could have existed otherwise, and their lives remain worth living, it appears the clones were not harmed — the same paradox as Sarah conceiving Kira young and disadvantaged. After surveying Boonin's conclusion that every escape route from the paradox fails and Benatar's antinatalist extreme, the chapter adopts Rivka Weinberg's solution that existence is a condition rather than a conferred good, so the wrong lies in knowingly making a person a means to eugenic ends. The Leda dance party at the end of Season Two, where each clone dances in her own style, shows the book's verdict: the clones' lives are worth living on their own terms, exactly as they fight to live them.

Treats Project Leda's monitors as data gatherers in a botched social-scientific experiment, contrasting the Mill/Durkheim prediction paradigm (social science modeled on physics, seeking causes and regularities) with Max Weber's interpretive paradigm that seeks motives and understanding from the inside. Donnie's ignorance of the experiment and deep involvement in Alison's life skew his reports; Daniel and the clone-raised Rachel, who thinks of clones as property, ruin Rachel's role as the experiment's control group; and Delphine's love for Cosima makes her report selectively. The chapter concludes that Leda fails as science under both paradigms while trampling the informed-consent ethics owed to human subjects — the same project that got Alison's neighbor Aynsley killed.

Maps two ancient accounts of happiness onto the two clones we meet first. Cosima is the Aristotelian: like her fellow biologist Aristotle she holds that knowing truth for its own sake is essential to human flourishing, so she demands Sarah's briefcase ("the answers are in the briefcase"), studies a murdered sister's autopsy, and accepts Leekie's offer of unfettered research even inside Dyad. Alison is the Epicurean: happiness is the removal of pain and protection from threat, so she wants nothing to do with the C-word, hunts her monitor only to restore her safety, and signs Leekie's contract for the promise that her family will be left alone.

Takes the message Cosima decodes in the clones' DNA — "This organism and derivative genetic material is restricted intellectual property" — and asks whether Dyad can legally and morally own the Clone Club. The chapter walks through US patent law and the Supreme Court's Myriad Genetics decision (naturally occurring DNA unpatentable, synthetic cDNA patentable) and argues that because the Leda and Castor clones were genetically engineered, their modified sequences could fall under the synthetic exception, making ownership legally possible. Morally, though, it sides with self-ownership: people own the products of their labor but not people, so patenting clones would recreate the wrongs of slavery, down to who controls clone marriages and clone offspring.

Extends Walter Benjamin's analysis of art under mechanical reproduction to human cloning: as photography and film stripped artworks of their "aura" (their unique link to an origin) while democratizing art, cloning strips human beings of Hannah Arendt's "natality" — our connection to a unique beginning — while democratizing human nature itself. The chapter argues this is liberation, not loss: Sarah is as human as Felix or Kira, denying the clones' humanity would strip the naturally born of their own freedom ("Either Sarah and her sisters are human, or no one is"), and Tony Sawicki's chosen trans identity shows that once natality stops being destiny, authenticity and autonomy become possible for the first time. The only truly immoral path is Leda and Castor's — treating the bioengineered as property, as Rachel was raised to treat herself.

book: 103 - David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel
essays: 2. You Don’t Have to Be Stupid to Be Cool
5. Squawking Like a Pink Monkey Bird—What
9. When Jumpin’ Jack Flash Met Ziggy Stardust
samples: The editor's farewell argues that Bowie's greatness lay in relentless transformation joined to honesty: unlike acts from Kiss to Miley Cyrus whose theatrics are mere spectacle 'in an Aristotelian sense,' Bowie's characters (Ziggy, the Thin White Duke, simulating fellatio with Mick Ronson) opened a discussion of gender and 'the multiple ways of being in the world.' Tracing the career from parents' fear of rock through the Eno-shaped Berlin trilogy's symbolist minimalism and the despised continuity of 'Changes,' it reads The Next Day as a defacement of 'Heroes' and Blackstar as a Mapplethorpe-like series of self-portraits made while unflinchingly facing death.

Reisch argues Bowie's parade of characters (Ziggy, Aladdin Sane, the Diamond Dogs persona) was never metaphysical chameleonry but a postwar, cold-war project: by crediting himself only as 'the actor' and calling Dylan out as Robert Zimmerman's artifice, Bowie exposed the 'denim and hippies' authenticity cult as itself a construction. Diamond Dogs' '1984' and 'Big Brother' tie this to the era's totalitarian nightmares of manipulable humanity, and Sartre's 'Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself' becomes 'the first principle of Bowie' - only constant reinvention keeps us from being fooled by ourselves or others, even at the anguished cost of 'Who Can I Be Now?'

Botz-Bornstein argues Bowie's coolness was an ethico-aesthetic achievement: an awkward, thin Bromley boy who, through hard training with mime Lindsay Kemp, kabuki discipline, and Kansai Yamamoto's costumes, stylized his very body movements - Nietzsche's 'wisdom of the body' over the intellect - into an honest attitude rather than a pose. The chapter explains his 'kitsch-cool' ability to manipulate kitsch (the 'Over the Rainbow' octave of 'Starman,' glam space futures) without being absorbed, reading it through Shuzo Kuki's Japanese aesthetic of iki, whose astringent negation 'cools' the sweet, and contrasts Bowie's playful, virtual transgression with the jihadi's 'worst kitsch' of heroic death.

Ammon asks whether anything persists beneath Bowie's serial personas, staging Parmenides's denial of change (with Zeno's paradoxes) and Descartes's melting wax against the Heraclitean flux of 'ch-ch-ch-changes.' Rejecting soul-substance views, he takes the empiricist line - Hume's introspection finds only particular perceptions, never a self - warns via the intentional fallacy (Manson's 'Helter Skelter,' Bloom's hawk) against letting Bowie's own pronouncements fix his songs' meanings, and tests 'meaning is use' on Bowie's calling rock stars fascists. Recurring undercurrents (dancing, apocalypse, distrust of authority) survive, but the conclusion is that Bowie's essence just is flux, 'the river we can't step into twice.'

Auxier reads Bowie's persona changes through Arthur Danto's philosophy of art: Warhol's 1964 Brillo Box ended art history by handing the power to decide what is art to the Art World's theories, and made celebrity itself an art form that Bowie then adopted - hiring Warhol's Pork cast to invent Ziggy and trading his person for a sequence of personas as performance art. By Danto's criterion of embodied meaning Bowie qualifies as an artist, yet the Art World still refuses him the title it grants Warhol, and the chapter closes by conceding that the Brillo Box changed the world while Bowie's works only showed how it had already been changed.

Littmann argues Bowie's surreal lyrics are a deliberate nonsense literature descended from Lear, Carroll, the Goons, Dylan, psychedelia, Beat poetry, and absurdist theatre, and that the obscurity does work: cryptic strokes paint larger worlds, voice fractured minds and alienation (Major Tom's 'little green wheels'), and leave interpretation to the listener, so each generation can read itself into songs like 'Moonage Daydream.' The hard question is evaluative - how can art whose effect depends on audience imagination be assessed at all? - and he answers that Bowie's forty-five years of popularity across shifting fashions is strong evidence the nonsense taps something of genuine, lasting artistic value.

book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!
essays: 6. Driven by Love to Go to War
14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.

Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.

Brendan Shea takes the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species (Homo flameus versus Homo sapiens) seriously and tests it first against Aristotle's essentialism—species fixed by necessary properties, complete with the doctrine of natural slaves—and then against three modern species concepts (Mayr's interbreeding criterion, the phylogenetic common-ancestry view, and the ecological-niche view), showing each gives the Jackal ambiguous or inconvenient verdicts, from sterile Pinks to horizontal gene transfer. He concludes with Peter Singer that moral equality never depended on equal intelligence or strength: Reds have interests just as Golds do, so enslaving them would be wrong even if Adrius were right about the biology. The deeper lesson is that the Jackal reasoned backwards from his commitment to Gold rule, finding whatever differences his prejudice needed—a warning against 'discovering' biological support for pre-existing biases.

Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.

Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.

Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.
